name: AOP-Wiki full XML snapshot (offline AOP graph)
what: Official quarterly/nightly XML download of the entire AOP-Wiki (all AOPs, key events, key-event relationships, prototypical stressors) plus nightly TSVs (aop_ke_mie_ao, aop_ke_ker, aop_ke_ec); also a paginated JSON API (/aops.json). Default license CC BY-SA 4.0, so content may be shipped inside an offline app with attribution; ARR-licensed AOPs auto-convert to BY-SA after a 30-day grace period per the 2026 release notes.
why_better: Old plan treats literature as unstructured text; AOPs are pre-built causal chains (MIE -> key events -> neurodegeneration AO) with evidence-quality levels per relationship, so the explainer retrieves the exact mechanistic pathway behind an NTI hit (e.g., oxidative stress -> mitochondrial damage) instead of hoping a chunk contains it -> grounded, pathway-level explanations with explicit confidence.
evidence: Download endpoints, API and release 2.8 (2026-03-08) notes fetched live. Exact AOP count: unverified (site blocks row scraping).
license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (default; some AOPs ARR during development)
fit_small_data: high - self-contained structured corpus of hundreds of AOPs, no labels needed, ships as one gzipped XML.
fit_onnx_cpu: high - XML parsed into chunks/graph once at install; no model needed to store it.
risk: XML schema (AopXml) changes between quarterly releases; pin a version. ARR-licensed AOPs must be filtered at snapshot time.

name: OECD TG 426 / TG 443 and 2023 DNT in vitro battery guidance (curated endpoint digest)
what: The regulatory anchor documents: TG 426 (in chemico neurotoxicity), TG 443 (in vitro battery characterisation of neurotoxicity), and the 2023 OECD DNT in vitro battery guidance. OECD site (oecd.org publications) returned 403 to automated fetch and no Wayback capture was found for the TG 443 entry page, so page count is unverified; iLibrary guidelines are typically 100-300 page PDFs (unverified).
why_better: An explainer that cannot name the TG 426/443 endpoint its NTI component maps to (e.g., acetylcholinesterase inhibition, mitochondrial membrane potential) fails the lab's actual 'why does this score mean that' question; embedding guideline PDFs as-is would fail because they are non-CC-licensed -> curate a project-authored plain-text digest of endpoints/acceptance criteria (our own writing, our license) and link back to the originals.
evidence: Unverified - could not fetch the OECD pages (HTTP 403); existence of TG 426/443 and the 2023 DNT guidance is per the project brief, not re-confirmed from a source in this session.
source_title: OECD Series on Testing and Assessment (iLibrary)
license: OECD copyright - full text NOT redistributable for bundling; short excerpts with attribution only
fit_small_data: high - a few documents; the value is curation into endpoint-level snippets.
fit_onnx_cpu: high - a few hundred KB of text; trivial.
risk: Legal: do not bundle OECD PDFs; keep digest + link. Content drift if OECD revises TG 443.

name: PMC Open Access Subset + Europe PMC (literature mirrors)
what: NIH PMC archive holds 12.4M articles (verified on pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov home); the OA Subset is the CC-licensed slice, retrievable via PMC Cloud Service/OAI-PMH/E-utilities/BioC (legacy FTP/AWS article-dataset distribution is being retired Aug 2026 - verified in 'New in PMC'). License varies per article (CC0/CC-BY/CC-BY-NC); commercial bundling requires filtering to CC0/CC-BY with attribution. Europe PMC (EBI) mirrors PMC plus additional OA journals and exposes full text via REST web services, but europepmc.org currently 403s automated fetch, so only the archived Web Service Reference PDF was confirmable - current endpoints unverified. Ship a pre-filtered neurotoxicity slice (e.g., PC12/SH-SY5Y/oxidative stress queries), plausibly 50k-300k articles (unverified exact count).
why_better: Old plan has no literature layer at all; a filtered OA slice gives the explainer citable primary evidence (dose, time-point, cell model) for every mechanistic claim, and JATS XML gives clean section-level chunks -> per-claim citations with PMID/PMCID instead of hallucinated references. Europe PMC as second mirror cross-checks by PMCID and adds non-PMC OA content -> higher recall for the same slice budget and a fallback if PMC's 2026 cutover breaks ingest.
evidence: PMC home states '12.4 million articles', 3039 full-participation journals (fetched 2026-09-27). OA neurotoxicity slice size: unverified. Europe PMC scale/endpoints: unverified (403).
source_title: PMC Open Access Subset / Europe PMC Web Service Reference (archived)
license: per-article CC (CC0/CC-BY/CC-BY-NC); PMC terms make users solely responsible for compliance; Europe PMC per-article terms + EBI access terms need a one-page legal check
fit_small_data: medium - slice must be built and pruned at build time; small relative to the app but the filter pipeline takes work.
fit_onnx_cpu: high - pre-chunked plain text at install; retrieval is vector+BM25 only.
risk: License-filtering errors (shipping CC-BY-NC or non-OA articles); PMC 2026 distribution cutover (FTP/OA Web Service/legacy AWS files removed) means ingest must use the new PMC Cloud Service layout; dedup against Europe PMC by PMCID mandatory.

name: PubChem + EPA CompTox/ToxCast/NTP/EFSA (per-compound reference cards)
what: PubChem is NIH's 'world's largest free chemistry database' (verified homepage tagline); US Government work, public-domain data with citation requested. Pull the three compound records (identity, XLogP, LD50, toxicity annotations, literature citations) as a few KB of structured cards per compound. EPA's CompTox Chemicals Dashboard confirms '1,376,722 Chemicals' (last updated October 2025) aggregating Tox21/ToxCast battery data; NTP/ToxCast microsites (ntp.gov, ntp.cancer.gov, toxcast.epa.gov) were unreachable from this environment (DNS failures) and EFSA's neurotoxicity topic page 404'd, so their sizes/term details are unverified. CompTox aggregates third-party submissions whose redistribution terms must be checked per data source.
why_better: Old plan's explainer has no chemical-level context; compact per-compound cards let the LLM ground every answer in the tested substance's physicochemical and known-toxicity profile -> dose/compound confusables (e.g., curcumin's antioxidant vs pro-oxidant data) resolved from retrieved facts, and the lab's battery design can be contextualized against the ToxCast/Tox21 assay space it mirrors -> the NTI stops being a bare number and becomes interpretable against a known battery landscape.
evidence: CompTox: 1,376,722 chemicals (fetched, meta description, Oct 2025). PubChem record count: unverified. NTP/EFSA details: unverified (unreachable/404).
license: US Gov data (public domain) but third-party-contributed records carry their own terms - legal review before bundling; EFSA opinions are CC-BY-NC in general (unverified here)
fit_small_data: high - 3 fixed compounds, static at install, refreshed manually.
fit_onnx_cpu: high - a handful of structured JSON rows.
risk: License ambiguity on contributed/third-party data; attribute source-tox links rather than restating them as agency fact. NTP/EFSA treated as watch until a clean fetch succeeds.

name: OpenStax Biology 2e / LibreTexts open neurobiology chapters (fundamentals corpus)
what: OpenStax publishes free college textbooks under CC-BY 4.0 (Biology 2e is the flagship; openstax.org detail pages fetched but the SPA did not render chapter content, so exact page count unverified, ~1,300+ pages expected). LibreTexts reports 3,000+ textbooks / 1.5M+ pages of OER content, mostly CC-licensed with per-page license metadata; a curated set of ~100-300 pages of neuro/neurochemistry chapters suffices.
why_better: Explainers aimed at non-expert stakeholders need plain-language definitions (axon, myelin, mitochondrial membrane potential) that neither OECD PDFs nor PMC abstracts provide; CC-BY OER chapters can be shipped and quoted -> every technical term in an NTI explanation can expand into a cited definition, the cheapest win for lay readability.
evidence: LibreTexts homepage: 3000+ textbooks, 300K+ homework questions, 1.5M+ pages (fetched). OpenStax Biology 2e chapter count: unverified.
license: CC-BY 4.0 (OpenStax); per-page CC variants on LibreTexts
fit_small_data: high - curate ~100-300 pages of neuro chapters.
risk: Lowest authority tier in the corpus - rank below OECD/AOP/PMC in retrieval weights; verify per-page CC-BY (not NC) before bundling for a commercial app.

name: NCBI Bookshelf (StatPearls, 'Basic Neurochemistry') and classic copyrighted textbooks - reference only
what: Bookshelf is NCBI's book archive; its site sits behind a reCAPTCHA wall for automated fetch, so per-title license text (Basic Neurochemistry, StatPearls chapters) could not be verified here. The MedRAG project (arXiv:2402.13178) uses StatPearls as a corpus and explicitly states it cannot redistribute StatPearls content per StatPearls' privacy policy - a direct signal that bundling is restricted. Classic neurotoxicology textbooks (Purves 'Neuroscience' Sinauer/McGraw-Hill; Casarett & Doull; Klaassen) are all-rights-reserved; publisher pages did not resolve cleanly from this environment, so edition/page details are unverified.
why_better: Both families are the field's canonical expert prose but cannot be legally bundled; the honest move is cite-only integration (chapter/section pointers, fair-use short quotes) plus the team's own summaries -> keeps the corpus legal while still giving users a 'read this chapter' pointer, and prevents the common failure of an offline app shipping scraped textbook chunks and creating a takedown risk.
evidence: MedRAG statpearls dataset card: 'According to the privacy policy of StatPearls, we are not allowed to distribute the StatPearls content. Please download the raw data from NCBI Bookshelf' (fetched via HF API). Bookshelf license page and textbook editions: unverified (reCAPTCHA/DNS failures).
source_title: MedRAG statpearls dataset card / NCBI Bookshelf
license: mixed; StatPearls not redistributable per MedRAG dataset card; other Bookshelf titles vary; classic textbooks all-rights-reserved
fit_small_data: low - only individual chapters with permissive licenses qualify for bundling.
fit_onnx_cpu: high - whatever is licensed, it's small text.
risk: High legal risk if bundled without per-title verification; keep to citations and short fair-use quotes.

name: Qwen3-8B (GGUF) via llama.cpp as the offline explainer LLM
what: Qwen3 dense models 0.6B-32B, Apache-2.0 (technical report + Qwen3-8B-GGUF HF card, official GGUF Q4_K_M ~5.0 GB, 32K context, thinking/non-thinking modes). Runtime is llama.cpp (MIT, 130k+ stars): 1.5-8 bit GGUF quantization, AVX/AVX2/AVX512 CPU support, OpenAI-compatible llama-server, CPU+GPU hybrid offload if the A5000/A6000 is available. Alternatives verified this session: Gemma 3 (1-27B, 'gemma' license, gated, 128K context, Gemma3-4B-IT competitive with Gemma2-27B-IT), Phi-4/Phi-4-mini (MIT, 14B/3.8B, strong per size), Llama 3.1/3.3-Instruct (proprietary community license, gated - fine for internal use, weaker for redistribution).
why_better: Old plan assumed generic local LLMs; an Apache-2.0 8B GGUF is the only class that is (a) legally bundleable, (b) fast enough at Q4 on a desktop CPU for interactive 'explain this NTI' latency, and (c) strong enough at instruction following to emit citation-tagged structured output via llama-server's OpenAI-compatible endpoint -> a per-answer explain loop instead of static templates, with Gemma-3-4B (low-RAM) and Phi-4-mini as fallbacks.
evidence: Qwen3 report: SOTA vs larger MoE/proprietary models on its benchmarks (no task-specific number restated). CPU tokens/s on the target lab PC: unverified - must benchmark on hardware.
license: Apache-2.0 (Qwen3); MIT (llama.cpp); gemma (Gemma 3); MIT (Phi-4); llama3.1/llama3.3 community licenses (Llama)
fit_small_data: high - no training; pure inference over the local corpus.
fit_onnx_cpu: high - GGUF+llama.cpp is the canonical CPU path for decoder LLMs; ONNX Runtime is better reserved for the encoder models (embeddings/reranker).
risk: Q4 8B needs ~5-6 GB RAM - 16 GB RAM PC is the floor; llama.cpp moves fast, pin a release tag; spot-check quantization quality on rare toxicology terms.

name: BGE-M3 (hybrid dense+sparse embedder, single model)
what: BAAI bge-m3: one XLM-RoBERTa-based model (1024-d, up to 8192-token context, MIT license, ONNX export per HF card) that simultaneously emits dense vectors, sparse lexical weights (BM25-like) and multi-vector ColBERT outputs; authors recommend 'hybrid retrieval + re-ranking' and report new SOTA on MIRACL/MKQA/MLDR (long-document) benchmarks, with BM25 remaining competitive for long docs. Alternatives verified this session: e5-large-v2 (MIT, ONNX-tagged), nomic-embed-text-v1.5 (Apache-2.0, ONNX-tagged, MTEB scores in card), MedCPT (ncbi/* HF models, 'license:other' - NCBI terms, needs check; trained on 255M PubMed click logs, paper claims SOTA on six biomedical IR tasks), PubMedBERT (not re-verified this session - unverified).
why_better: Old-plan RAG would pair a dense embedder with a separate BM25 index; bge-m3 produces the sparse weights in the same forward pass -> hybrid retrieval with zero extra infra, which matters because neurotoxicity queries are keyword-heavy ('TG 443', 'PC12', 'IC50 doxorubicin') where pure-dense retrieval is weakest, so hybrid retrieval measurably improves recall of guideline/assay chunks. If A/B favors domain over versatility, MedCPT is the biomedical-tuned challenger.
evidence: Paper/model card: SOTA on multilingual and long-document retrieval benchmarks (MIRACL, MKQA, MLDR); exact numbers not restated. Retrieval on this corpus: unverified - measure.
source_title: M3-Embedding: Multi-Linguality, Multi-Functionality, Multi-Granularity Text Embeddings
license: MIT (model+code); e5 MIT; nomic Apache-2.0; MedCPT NCBI 'other' terms
fit_small_data: high - no fine-tuning needed; ~570M-param encoder embeds a 100k-chunk corpus in minutes on CPU.
fit_onnx_cpu: high - MIT + ONNX-exported; cap chunks at 512-1024 tokens for speed; verify parity of the ONNX sparse head (less exercised than the dense head).
risk: MedCPT's 'license:other' tag is a real blocker for shipping if unclear - default to MIT bge-m3, keep MedCPT as challenger. e5/nomic are viable but English-only and dense-only, strictly less capable here.

name: bge-reranker-v2-m3 (cross-encoder re-ranker)
what: 567.8M-param XLM-RoBERTa sequence-classification cross-encoder (Apache-2.0, ~17M HF downloads) from the BGE family, explicitly recommended by the bge-m3 authors for the post-retrieval stage; FlagEmbedding (MIT) ships inference and fine-tuning scripts for the whole embedding+reranker line.
why_better: Flat top-k retrieval returns plausible-but-wrong chunks (a doxorubicin-cardiotoxicity chunk for a neurotoxicity question); a 568M cross-encoder scoring each (query, chunk) pair reorders top-50 to top-8 -> the LLM sees fewer distractors, which the medical-RAG benchmark literature identifies as the dominant accuracy lever (context noise, lost-in-the-middle) -> cheaper accuracy gain than any LLM upgrade.
evidence: Parameter count 567,755,777 and Apache-2.0 from HF API (fetched). Reranking gain on this corpus: unverified - A/B against no-reranker on the eval set.
fit_small_data: high - no training; scores ~30-100 candidate chunks per query.
fit_onnx_cpu: high - one forward pass per pair; 30-100 passes per query is seconds on CPU; XLM-R ONNX export is routine.
risk: Latency on low-end CPUs if rerank budget is large - cap at top-30. Optional later: fine-tune on ~200 team relevance judgments.

name: sqlite-vec (+ FTS5 BM25) as the offline hybrid vector store
what: Mozilla-sponsored pure-C SQLite extension (Apache-2.0/MIT, 8.1k stars) storing float/int8/binary vectors in vec0 virtual tables with KNN queries, embeddable in a desktop app alongside FTS5 BM25 and metadata SQL; pre-v1 (breaking changes possible), ANN benchmark suite in repo. At <1M chunks brute-force KNN is already fast on CPU, so no HNSW needed. Alternatives verified: FAISS (MIT, 41k stars - separate index files, no SQL/metadata joins, weaker embedded-deployment story) and LanceDB (Apache-2.0, 11.5k stars, embedded Rust columnar+vector+SQL - the strongest FAISS-style alternative).
why_better: A vector DB server or sidecar is overkill for an offline desktop app; sqlite-vec puts vectors, chunk text and metadata in ONE portable SQLite file the app already needs -> hybrid dense+BM25+metadata filtering (e.g., 'only OECD-source chunks') is a single SQL query, and the whole corpus is one file to ship, back up and version. FAISS/LanceDB lose the metadata-join and single-file properties.
evidence: Repo verified (licenses, pure C, KNN API, benchmarks). Recall/latency vs FAISS/LanceDB at this scale: unverified - benchmark, but exact search at <1M vectors is the accuracy upper bound anyway.
fit_small_data: high - overkill-proof at our scale; exact search, no index build.
fit_onnx_cpu: high - pure C SQLite, zero native deps beyond SQLite itself.
risk: pre-v1 API churn; Windows packaging of a compiled SQLite extension needs care. Fallback: FAISS (flat index) if packaging bites.

name: ALCE-style citation-grounded generation (anti-hallucination guardrail)
what: ALCE (arXiv:2305.14627) is the benchmark+method family for LLMs generating text with citations, with automatic metrics for fluency, correctness and citation quality (support/recall/precision) correlated with human judgment; its key finding: even the best 2023 models lacked complete citation support 50% of the time on ELI5. Concretely: prompt the local LLM to emit [chunk-id] spans, then verify each at runtime - drop or flag any claim whose cited chunk does not support it (support check = embedding similarity of claim vs cited chunk, reusing bge-m3).
why_better: Old plan has no hallucination control for the explainer; citation verification converts 'sounds plausible' into 'every sentence traceable to a shipped chunk' -> the app can hard-fail an answer instead of silently inventing a dose or an AOP, the one failure mode a lab will not forgive in a toxicity tool.
evidence: ELI5: best models lack complete citation support 50% of the time (paper, 2023). Post-guardrail rate with an 8B local model: unverified - measure on the eval set.
source_title: Enabling Large Language Models to Generate Text with Citations (ALCE)
fit_small_data: high - no data beyond the chunk store; pure prompting + verification code.
fit_onnx_cpu: high - verification is embedding similarity, no extra model.
risk: Small local LLMs are weaker at well-formed citation spans - needs prompt engineering + a repair pass. Over-strict verification produces 'no answer'; tune the support threshold on the eval set.

name: RAGAS (reference-free RAG evaluation harness)
what: RAGAS (arXiv:2309.15217; repo now vibrantlabsai/ragas, Apache-2.0, ~16k stars) provides reference-free metrics - faithfulness, answer relevancy, context precision/recall - evaluable with LLM-as-judge, plus auto test-set generation and experiment tracking; it integrates with local LLMs via OpenAI-compatible endpoints (llama-server qualifies).
why_better: Old plan had no RAG evaluation; without metrics, tuning chunk size, hybrid weights and rerank budget is guesswork. RAGAS gives per-component scores (retrieval vs generation) so the team knows whether a bad answer is a retrieval miss or an LLM failure -> targeted fixes instead of re-rolling the pipeline.
evidence: Framework verified (repo+paper). Judge-model validity with an 8B local judge: unverified - treat scores as relative between versions, not absolute.
source_title: Ragas: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation
fit_small_data: high - no corpus dependency; needs a ~50-100 Q&A gold set (hand-build from TG 443 endpoints + AOPs).
fit_onnx_cpu: medium - LLM-as-judge runs on the local 8B; fine as a nightly batch, slow interactively.
risk: LLM-as-judge with a small judge model is noisy; use for regression tracking between versions, not absolute quality claims.

name: MIRAGE / MedRAG (biomedical RAG benchmark + toolkit)
what: MIRAGE (arXiv:2402.13178, 'Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine') is a 7,663-question benchmark from five medical QA datasets, evaluated across 41 retriever/LLM combinations with the MedRAG toolkit; its HF org (MedRAG/pubmed 23.9M snippets, /textbooks 18 medical textbooks, /statpearls, /wikipedia) publishes the exact corpora and <=1000-token chunking. (The general RAG benchmark MIRAGE, arXiv:2504.17137, 7,560 questions/37,800-pool, is the namesake; the medical one is the relevant source here.)
why_better: Generic RAG benchmarks don't measure what a neurotoxicity explainer fails at (dose/context confusion, lost-in-the-middle over long guideline sections); MIRAGE's methodology - multiple corpora, multiple retrievers, context-noise metrics - plus its findings (RAG improves six LLMs by up to 18% over CoT prompting, log-linear scaling, lost-in-the-middle in medical RAG) tell the team which corpus/retriever combinations to prioritize before building -> the evaluation design is borrowed, not invented.
evidence: 7,663 questions; 1.8T prompt tokens; up to 18% accuracy gain elevating GPT-3.5/Mixtral to GPT-4 level (paper). PubMed corpus subset: 23.9M snippets (HF card). Neurotoxicity-specific numbers: unverified - build a private 50-100 Q eval set.
license: benchmark code/data per HF org (PubMed-derived chunks - check terms when reusing the exact files)
fit_small_data: medium - the benchmark is external; the reusable parts are methodology + the private domain eval set we build.
fit_onnx_cpu: medium - full MIRAGE evaluation with a local 8B is a long batch job (use the A5000/A6000 box for this).
risk: MedRAG code repo location not confirmed in this session (github.com/microsoft/MedRAG 404'd; HF org confirmed) - locate the toolkit before committing. USMLE medical domain differs from regulatory neurotoxicity - weight the private eval set above the public one.

name: LightRAG (graph-based RAG with citations and offline deployment mode)
what: HKUDS LightRAG (MIT, ~40k stars, EMNLP 2025; arXiv:2410.05779) builds an LLM-extracted knowledge graph with dual-level (low/high) retrieval over the corpus, supports citations (added 2025.03), rerankers (2025.08), and ships an explicit Offline Deployment guide for air-gapped environments; the paper reports improvements in retrieval accuracy and efficiency vs flat-vector RAG. Heavier predecessor GraphRAG (arXiv:2404.16130, MIT) is now in Microsoft maintenance mode.
why_better: Neurotoxicity 'why' questions are multi-hop (chemical -> MIE -> key events -> AO -> observed morphology), where flat chunk retrieval fragments the answer; LightRAG's graph index - seeded for free by the AOP-Wiki corpus since that graph is given, not LLM-mined - retrieves the whole chain in one pass -> coherent multi-step mechanistic explanations. This is the ambitious upgrade beyond the old plan's flat-chunk RAG.
evidence: Paper: 'considerable improvements in retrieval accuracy and efficiency compared to existing approaches' on its test sets; no neurotoxicity-specific numbers (unverified).
source_title: LightRAG: Simple and Fast Retrieval-Augmented Generation
fit_small_data: medium - graph indexing with an 8B local LLM is the expensive part; restrict graph extraction to the AOP+OECD+compound-card subset (~10k chunks) and keep literature as flat vectors.
fit_onnx_cpu: medium - retrieval is fast (graph lookups + vectors); the indexing LLM phase is slow on CPU but is a one-time build job.
risk: Heaviest engineering item; indexing with a local 8B LLM is slow and small-model extraction quality is weaker than GPT-class (repo notes improvements with open models, no parity claim). Phase 2, after flat RAG ships.
